full_text:
I’m changing the format of my annual fantasy football Draft Plan article this year and have decided to separate my actual plan from the detailed write-ups I do on my key player targets. I don’t think the Draft Plan article will suffer at all, since I’ll be naming all the players I’m targeting in the article, as usual. I just think the article got too large and cumbersome, so I’ll be publishing (and constantly updating) my entire player target list with analysis in this new “Guru’s Guys” article.

Make no mistake: while the Draft Plan is critical, I view my player targets as the most important part of the plan, and therefore the most important thing I do in the preseason. In the past, I’ve isolated about 70 of the top 300 players for my target list, but I’m getting even more selective with age. Lately, I’ve narrowed the list down to 50 players, or only 25% of the top-200 players, and this year I’m down even further to only 35.

Before I get into the players, here’s a checklist of my criteria, so you know exactly what I’m looking for in my player targets:

1.  __Value__ — To break it down in its most basic form, I’m mostly looking for players who I believe will outproduce their draft positions (ADP). The more expensive a player is, the harder it is for him to make it onto my list. I generally do not include consensus top-12 overall picks on my list of player targets.

+   __Production and role__ — For players I think are appropriately priced, I need to be confident in their ability to produce and their volume/role. For RBs, versatility is a huge factor. For pass-catchers, things like target share, first-read target share, etc., are hugely important, and scheme also matters here.
+   __Infrastructure__ — Ideally, a player target of mine is in a stable organization. I’m looking for continuity with positive coaching and play-calling in a proven system with a strong supporting cast (especially a quality offensive line).
+   __Age and durability__ — I greatly value youth and tend to be ageist, but I will make some exceptions when an older player is generally durable and relatively affordable.

As you can see, my standards are high. With only 32 players out of 200 on my list this year, I’m weeding out over 85% of the player pool, so a player needs to check a lot of positive boxes for me to back him. __I’ll surely add some more players to my list in August, but I’m hoping my selectivity leads to better accuracy.__

\> *__Note__**: I’m listing the players in order of ADP, but I’ll also rank the players based on my ideal order of preference below.*

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Quarterback Targets__

__{{Justin Herbert|QB|LAC|21681}}__ (LAC, 87) — While they don’t run off a ton of plays, the __Jim Harbaugh__/__Mike McDaniel__ marriage should be magical, especially with their excellent OTs back and healthy. In 2022, __Tua Tagovailoa__, with noticeable limitations and all, led the NFL in TD percentage (6.3%) and YPA (8.9), and in 2023, he led in passing yards (4624) under McDaniel. The selection of speedy WR __Brenen Thompson__, which I [predicted on the FP Podcast before the Draft](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/episode/kc-concepcion-nick-singleton-jadarian-price-or-afc-landing-spots-for-2026-nfl-draft#/), could give them the lid-lifter they’ve lacked and complete their (already solid) receiving corps. LA then added veteran TE __David Njoku__, giving Herbert a fully-stocked receiving corps with 6-7 strong options. Herbert last year was tied for 5th in rushing attempts (83) and second in rushing yards (498) last year, so I think we can count on top-7 rushing production with the offense in the hands of two strong offensive minds who are run-oriented. He played behind a decimated OL all season, so Herbert was only 17th in FP/DB, yet he was also still 7th in catchable throw percentage. He’s only the eighth or ninth QB off the board this summer, but with better health around him this year, he should slice and dice NFL defenses, continue to rush the ball 5-6 times a game, and post top-7 fantasy digits.

{{PAYWALL}}

__{{Trevor Lawrence|QB|JAX|22490}}__ (Jax, 90) — Lawrence’s ADP of QB11 is beyond reasonable for a player who looked like the best QB in the league down the stretch and who ranked *first* in FPG (23.5) the final 10 weeks of 2025. Lawrence’s YPA and completion rates were identical to the year before, so his production was boosted by his 9 TDs on the ground (7 in the final 10 weeks). But he scattered 12 rushing TDs over his previous three seasons, and the ground production should continue in an improved offense that was 6th in Points For under new HC __Liam Coen__. Lawrence looked more comfortable than ever under Coen, especially after Coen simplified the offense and advised his QB to “let it rip” in a Week 10 pep talk, which he did. He’ll likely need to keep running in TDs to give you spike weeks, but this offense is likely still ascending with a full year of __Jakobi Meyers__ and with __Brian Thomas__ seemingly incapable of playing as poorly as he did last year. Lawrence had the second-highest drop percentage in the league (8.6%) and the most dropped yards (397), per FP Data, but the vibes have been great on Thomas, Meyers, __Parker Washington__, and the recently-extended TE __Brenton Strange__.

__{{Brock Purdy|QB|SF|23241}}__ (SF, 104) — I’ve been into Purdy in each of his last four seasons, and while it hasn’t gone swimmingly due to injuries, he’s profitable when he plays, as evidenced by his QB5 standing in FPG last season (21.0). Over the last three seasons, Purdy is first in EPA/DB, fifth in FP/DB, third in FP/opportunity, and fifth in FPG. Purdy got his TD percentage back up to 7% in 2025 after dropping to 4.4% in 2024, but last season was in line with his other two campaigns in which he posted a 7.4% and 7.0% TD rate. Purdy in 2025 was tied for second in FP/DB with __Lamar Jackson__, and his passing and rushing production in nine games put him on a 17-game pace of 43 TDs (37.5 passing, 5.6 rushing). This is an older roster with more than its fair share of injury concerns, but Purdy still has all-world LT __Trent Williams__, and Big __Mike Evans__ should help keep the TDs coming. As only the QB14 off the board this year, he *has* to remain on my short list of value targets at the position.

__{{Tyler Shough|QB|NO|23187}}__ (NO, 132) — I default to trusting a play-caller with a proven track record, and that is HC __Kellen Moore__. From Week 10 on (eight games), the rookie Shough was the QB8 in FPG, thanks partly to 3 TDs on the ground. But he also had a strong 69.7% completion rate with a solid 7.7 YPA in that span, which was better than __Josh Allen__. Excluding first-reads, designed throws, and checkdowns last year, Shough actually had the league’s highest adjusted net yards/attempt (10.94), which is a great sign. I’m concerned about a year-two speed bump for an overachieving first-year QB with a small NFL sample size, since the league tends to catch up with them quickly (see: __C.J. Stroud__). But I’m satisfied with Moore’s acumen and the upgrades they made to their receiving corps, adding a potential “one” in __Jordyn Tyson__ and a potential needle-mover at TE in __Oscar Delp__. They have two recent top-15 overall picks at OT, and they also added a back in __Travis Etienne,__ who was second in the league with 6 receiving TDs last year. Shough is 6 '5”, athletic, and he has a good arm, so if he flops, it’ll likely be due to an injury (which has been a problem for Shough in the past). When he’s on the field, his floor should be solid, and his ceiling could be higher than the masses believe.

__{{Kyler Murray|QB|MIN|20889}}__ (Min, 134) — The Vikings are “my team,” and in the past, my fandom has boosted my accuracy in handicapping their players. That said, I blame my __J.J. McCarthy__ and __T.J. Hockenson__ failures in ‘25 on hubris, since I made too many assumptions about a first-year starter. Granted, much of the analysis of McCarthy focused on his low price tag, and I had no idea that McCarthy’s OL would be ravaged by injuries all season. I *was* correct in thinking JJ would produce with his legs (he was eighth at QB with 4 rushing TDs in just 10 games), but my “gut” learned a lesson: backing a first-year starter with no body of work can be disastrous. My “gut” is once again very optimistic about the Vikings’ QB, but this time my optimism is keyed by Murray’s extensive body of work, which has mostly been productive for fantasy. Murray has some injury issues and limited height, and he’ll face a learning curve in a new offense and competition from McCarthy. But playing on a one-year “prove-it” deal for his favorite NFL team in a very good offense with excellent personnel should lead to strong production. Murray will certainly continue to use his legs, so his floor looks appealing. But as about the 20th QB off the board, he has a chance to shatter his preseason ADP, so his ceiling is as good as anyone drafted outside the top-12 at the position.

__{{Malik Willis|QB|MIA|23118}}__ (Mia, 146) — Miami is starting over with a new coaching staff and also a completely revamped receiving corps, so expectations are low for Willis. However, he’s become a viable threat with his arm — which is intriguing because he has a great one — and he’s a top athlete with elite rushing potential. He’s had four career games with 14 or more pass attempts, and he’s rushed for 40+ yards in all four with 4 TDs on the ground. Among 61 QBs with at least 35 attempts last year, Willis’ 1.11 FP/DB easily led the league, but it wasn’t just his running, since his 94.3% catchable throw rate was also tops in the league. New HC __Jeff Hafley__ was with Willis in Green Bay last season, and his new OC __Bobby Slowik__ comes from the same Shanahan tree as GB’s __Matt LaFleur__, so the scheme and offensive philosophy will be familiar to Willis. Willis getting to 3000 yards passing on the season may be too much to ask, but due to his running, he’s easily capable of posting top-15 digits while averaging fewer than 200 passing yards per game.

In terms of ranking these players by preference, my order is very similar to ADP's. I’d slot them like this:

+   (A) __Justin Herbert__ (LAC, 87)

+   (B) __Trevor Lawrence__ (Jax, 90)

Since these two are only separated by a few ADP slots, let’s call Herbert my #1A choice, with Lawrence being #1B and my immediate backup plan if Herbert is taken in front of me.

+   __Brock Purdy__ (SF, 104)

+   __Kyler Murray__ (Min, 134)
+   __Tyler Shough__ (NO, 132)
+   __Malik Willis__ (Mia, 146)

##### 200+ ADP guys I like

None.

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Running Back Targets__

__{{Saquon Barkley|RB|PHI|19766}}__ (Phi, 14) — For the record, I was very into Barkley in 2024, and very out on him in 2025, so I’m attempting to get Barkley right three years in a row. [As I mentioned here](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/gurus-best-bets-nfl-player-futures#/), as long as one of HC __Nick Sirianni’s__ flunkies isn’t running the offense, like in 2024 when Barkley had 10 rushing TDs and over 2500 yards from scrimmage, Philly is in good shape on that side of the ball. I don’t see a monster season incoming, but he’s been durable four years in a row, and we’re projecting Barkley to lead the league in carries. With the offense in better hands under well-respected new OC __Sean Mannion__, I’ll be queuing Barkley up in Round 2 if I open with a WR in Round 1.

__{{Chase Brown|RB|CIN|24374}}__ (Cin, 17) — I was apologizing for my affinity for Brown by late October, since he averaged just 3.65 YPC (RB71), 44.7% Success Rate (60th), and just 14.1 Expected Fantasy Points per game (RB18) from Weeks 1-7. But he finished the season as the RB8 in total points and FPG, which was above my preseason ranking. The Bengals did absolutely nothing in the backfield in the offseason, so Brown is 100% locked into a large role. He’s about the 10th back off the board, but we have him sixth in targets, receptions, and receiving yards, and he’s been a decent rushing TD guy with 13 in two seasons and a rushing score in three of his last five games last year. Expectations for the offense are high this season, so Brown could rack up more rushing TDs than expected, and his receiving work keeps his floor more than palatable. Brown’s also heading into the final year of his rookie contract, and while a contract extension could happen at any time, until he puts pen to paper on a new deal, he’s gunning for his first big payday in the NFL.

__{{Breece Hall|RB|NYJ|22526}}__ (NYJ, 30) — Breece has been a complicated evaluation the last two seasons due to his 2022 ACL tear and the fact that he plays for a dysfunctional organization. The dysfunction continued in 2025, and they got poor QB play from __Justin Fields__, __Tyrod Taylor__, and __Brady Cook__, but Hall and the Jets' running game actually had a solid year. He was tied for 11th in attempts with __Jamyr Gibbs__ (243), and NY was ninth in YBC/ATT, 11th in rushing YPG, and had the 5th-lowest stuff rate in the league. The Jets were dead last in rushing attempts inside the five, so Hall scored only 4 rushing TDs, and his 3.0 targets/game last year was by far the lowest total of his career. But among RBs with at least 10 catches, he was at least fifth with 9.7 YPR, and playing with a veteran QB in __Geno Smith__ (we hope) and for an experienced OC like __Frank Reich__ (Colts RBs combined for 99 receptions back in 2020 under Reich) should stabilize the offense. At around RB14, I’m buying Breece.

__{{Javonte Williams|RB|DAL|22558}}__ (Dal, 34) — I’ve been a Javonte enthusiast since Day One, but after his devastating 2022 knee injury and sluggish return in 2023-24, I was hesitant to back him in 2025. As it turned out, while he’s lost some juice since the injury, he’s still very good at football. He’s about the RB18 off the board at around 35 overall, which is a tad pricey. But if everyone’s scarfing up the backs, Javonte looks like a solid RB2 around the Round 3-4 turn if I’m feeling the need to go RB. He completely dominated the touches in the backfield last year with 287 in 16 games (17.9 per game), and he’s a sneaky bell-cow with little competition in the backfield again this year. We have the reliable Williams 11th in carries (249.6), but he may hit 275+ on the ascending Cowboys. His role in the passing game is underwhelming (so we’re only 22nd in receptions with 36), but he averaged 50 receptions a season in 2023-2024, so 40+ grabs is entirely possible.

__{{Cam Skattebo|RB|NYG|25887}}__ (NYG, 34) — Despite his uneventful summer in which he was slowed by a hamstring injury, I was in on Skattebo last year, and once the season started, I was glad I was. Skattebo had few problems pushing the pile in the NFL as a rookie, as his 2.82 YACO/ATT was fifth-best out of 65 RBs with at least 50 carries last year, and 69.5% of his rushing yards were after contact (second-best in the NFL). It’s clear that new HC __Jim Harbaugh__ wants the offense to be keyed by a power running game, which is why they brought in the bruising FB __Patrick Rickard__, the former Raven. Skattebo should be a good fit for new run-game maven __Greg Roman__, whose Chargers used zone concept runs at the 5th-lowest rate over the last two years (45.2%). Skattebo ranked just 36th of 49 qualifying RBs in success rate on zone concept runs (45.2%), but he was 8th-best on man/gap concept runs (59.0%). As for __Tyrone Tracy__, he ranked 3rd-worst of 40 RBs in success rate on man/gap concept runs (41.4%). It’s that scheme fit along with his receiving versatility and goal line opportunities that do it for me, but a healthy Skattebo could completely take over the backfield, and the fantasy ROI will be very nice if he does.

__{{David Montgomery|RB|HOU|20882}}__ (Hou, 51) — Fantasy Points is projecting 1115 rushing yards in 15 games on 263.2 carries (9th-most), so it looks like people are overrating backup __Woody Marks__ a bit. Houston was a 12-win playoff team last season with a struggling QB, and they have arguably the best defense in the league, so the durable Montgomery, who’s a good scheme fit in Houston, should easily clear 200 totes. Marks is a good receiver, but Montgomery is no slouch in the passing game, and he’s great at pass protection, so he should get a few targets every week. He’s not a sexy fantasy pick, but as about the 23rd back off the board, he’s a strong pick as an RB3 or even a viable RB2 for teams that load up on the other skill positions.

__{{D’Andre Swift|RB|CHI|17124}}__ (Chi, 55) — Swift has produced three years in a row, logging 223 or more carries in each season. His rushing data was strong last year, ranking top-15 among 49 RBs with 100 or more carries in rushing yards per game, YPC average, explosive run percentage, and success rate. He’s not tremendous in terms of yards gained after contact, and he’s mediocre on man/gap runs (4.16 YPC), but #2 man __Kyle Monangai__ should get the majority of those carries. 65.5% of Swift’s runs last year were on zone concepts (6th-most), and his 5.27 YPC on those runs was 6th-best, so I expect him to retain his primary role over Monangai. They also did absolutely nothing in the off-season to upgrade their RB room, and Fantasy Points is projecting another 200+ carries for Swift. The Bears have an issue at LT with starter __Ozzy Trapilo__ expected to miss most of the season, but Chicago’s running game and O-line are strong overall, posting the 6th-best in YBCO/Att (2.18) and ranking top-5 in attempts, rushing yards per game, YPC, and success rate, per Fantasy Points Data. I wouldn’t feel the need to select him as my RB3 at his ADP, but if I were still looking for my RB2 in Round 5, Swift is an excellent option.

__{{Chuba Hubbard|RB|CAR|21691}}__ (Car, 74) — Hubbard has been Mr. Every-Other-Year dating back to his college days, and a lot of his inconsistency is injury-related, so he might be due for a strong season, which he tends to have in even-numbered years. He suffered a Grade 2 calf strain in December of a breakout 2024 season, and then he dealt with another calf injury early in 2025, which opened the door for __Rico Dowdle__ to take over. Hubbard admitted that he came back too quickly, so it’s plausible that a clean bill of health this year leads to another big season. The Panthers were slightly below-average in terms of rushing volume last year, but I view them as a running team, and they blocked it up pretty well in ‘25, ranking 13th in YBC/Att with the 10th-best stuff rate. Their RBs had 400+ carries and 90+ targets, so even if __Jonathon Brooks__ is a factor all year, a relatively healthy Hubbard should log 225+ touches. Hubbard is just a season removed from an RB15 season with 293 touches and 11 TDs, so with Brooks actually passing him in ADP as of late-June, Hubbard looks like a strong value at RB28 off the board, and a great RB3 to draft in the 6th or 7th round.

__{{Rico Dowdle|RB|PIT|21952}}__ (Pit, 84) — We’re projecting Rico to finish 29th in carries (177), 29th in rush yards (785), and 27th in catches (32), so he looks like a small value even as he’s gone from the RB35 off the board in early June to the RB30 in late June. __Jaylen Warren__ has rushed for 100+ yards only four times in four seasons, something Dowdle did in four of his last five games as a Cowboy in 2024. Rico then ran for 206, 183, and 130 yards in a span of five weeks in 2025, so he’s a better workhorse than Warren. 2025 3rd-rounder __Kaleb Johnson__ was a bust in year one, and rookie __Eli Heidenreich__ is a runner/receiver hybrid, so Dowdle looks like the best early-down option for new HC __Mike McCarthy__, who certainly wants to pound the rock.

##### 200+ ADP guys I like

None.

\> __Note__: I realize this is a very low number of RB picks, especially of the late-round variety, but I’ll be adding to this list once training camps open and I get more information.

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Wide Receiver Targets__

__{{Nico Collins|WR|HOU|21756}}__ (Hou, 22) — Nico’s target percentages, targets per route run, and first-read target share have not been elite the last two seasons (top-15-20 range). But I still think he’s a top-10 fantasy wideout, and he’s a cleaner prospect than the other wideouts going off the board in his range, which is around 15-20 overall. It’s a little boring, and he’s not playing with an elite QB, but the Texans just gave him a raise in May while locking him in for the next two seasons, so he’s still the unquestioned “No. 1” here. His YPRR dropped from an elite 2.94 in 2024 to 2.44, but that’s still excellent and ranked 14th among all WR/TEs. Collins, fourth in receiving yards per game since 2024 (78.4), is, at worst, a solid floor/ceiling selection in the 15-25 range. Collins looks particularly appealing in Round 2 for teams that pick at the top of Round 1 and open with a RB.

__{{Chris Olave|WR|NO|22565}}__ (NO, 28) — He did have a blood clot in his lung that forced him to sit out the season finale last year, but Olave is expected to be 100% to open training camp, and that’s on the heels of an uber-productive 2025 season in which he avoided a concussion and played in 16 healthy games. Olave has always been on the frail side, but he’s put in a lot of extra work in the weight room this year and has added 8 to 10 pounds to his frame, which I certainly view as a positive. Olave clicked with QB __Tyler Shough__, as evidenced by the data. From Weeks 8-17, among 34 WRs with at least 50 targets, Olave was top-15 in YPRR (2.23), receptions (56), target percentage (26.2%), TPRR (.26), deep targets (21), first-read targets (34%), expected fantasy points per route-run (.47), to name several key metrics. He’ll have more target competition with __Jordyn Tyson__ added in the first round, but all signs point to Shough continuing to grow under HC __Kellen Moore__. If I opt to open with non-WRs in the first two rounds, Olave looks like an excellent target in Round 3.

__{{DeVonta Smith|WR|PHI|21687}}__ (Phi, 38) — There are a handful of players that I’m “in” on every single year, and DeVonta is on that short list. The results haven’t been stellar, but they have been extremely solid and steady. And Smith now takes the reins of the “No. 1” receiver role, which is notable because he was only 38th among 104 WRs/TEs with 50 or more targets in TPRR in 2025 (__A.J. Brown__ was 10th), yet Smith was 20th in receptions with 77 (Brown was 18th). Smith is the 17th WR off the board this summer, and the Eagles have some new toys to play with at receiver in rookie __Makai Lemon__, __Dontayvion Wicks__, and __Hollywood Brown__ (plus TE __Eli Stowers__), so fantasy drafters have kind of pigeonholed Smitty into the 4th round. But if you want a 4th-rounder who gives you 4th-round production with 3rd-round upside, Skinny Batman should be your man. Respected new OC __Sean Mannion__’s offense would have to completely flop for it to be as bad as 2025’s Eagles offense was, so Smith is getting an upgraded coaching staff and role in 2026.

__{{Terry McLaurin|WR|WAS|20873}}__ (Was, 50) — Opportunity is knocking for McLaurin, who is the only established wideout on the D.C. roster, and he’s due for a bounce-back after 2025 was disrupted by a training camp holdout and two subsequent lower-body injuries (likely related to his holdout). He missed over twice as many games last year (7) as his previous six seasons combined (3), and with no holdout concerns this year, McLaurin has looked healthy and re-energized by new OC __David Blough__’s offense. It’s a new system for everyone to learn, but McLaurin is the focal point (even if they sign a veteran like __Brandon Aiyuk__). In the past, McLaurin has been a little too static and locked into the Boundary X receiver role, but per McLaurin, the new offense will give them the flexibility to move around the formation. It’s great that __Jayden Daniels__ is healthy and ready to go, but it’s worth noting that McLaurin produced with backup __Marcus Mariota__ last year, so the QB room is solid.

__{{D.J. Moore|WR|BUF|19844}}__ (Buf, 56) — If the 29-year-old was a perfect prospect, he wouldn’t be joining his third team in five seasons, so Moore’s a polarizing pick at this point. But in Moore’s defense, he’s struggled with poor QB play in Carolina and Chicago. Of course, Moore averaged a whopping 97 receptions per game in 2023-2024 with __Justin Fields__ and (shaky) rookie __Caleb Williams__, so Moore’s upgrade at QB is significant. Even more encouraging, Moore posted two of his best seasons under new Bills HC __Joe Brady__, who was Carolina’s offensive coordinator in 2020-21, so the Bills know what they’re getting in the veteran, and Moore knows what he’s getting with his new OC. Moore got lost in the shuffle last year as new HC __Ben Johnson__ looked to feature their younger receivers, namely __Luther Burden__ and __Colston Loveland__, both of whom he drafted in 2025. But his role should not be a problem this year for Moore, who was only 37th in target share and 69th in TPRR at WR last year out of 76 WRs with at least 50 targets. QB play shouldn’t be an issue, either, since he goes from Williams, who ranked 40th in catchable throw rate (69.4%) out of 45 QBs, to Allen, who ranked fourth (79.1%). Allen’s pass attempts have dropped three years in a row and were down to a paltry 460 last year, but Moore ranked ninth in designed target share (17.1%) last season, and he’s been a good TD guy with 27 TDs his last four seasons with a strong 8.79% TD rate on his catches. I see Moore as a viable WR2 this year, but he can probably be had as a WR3 in the 5th or 6th round.

__{{Rome Odunze|WR|CHI|24977}}__ (Chi, 61) — One of my biggest deliberations this off-season has been differentiating between Odunze and second-year man __Luther Burden__, and with cost a serious consideration, I’m going with Odunze as the preferred pick. Burden is intriguing, but I’m not buying his pricey ADP because he benefited too much from a handful of huge plays and a lot of manufactured touches. His lingering foot issue is a legit concern, so I’ll be bailing on Odunze if it’s still an issue in camp this summer. But if he’s able to practice and the vibes are good, then it’s wheels up for a guy who was actually the WR3 in scoring with 20/296/5 Weeks 1-4 before the injury. He’s not really a volume receiver, as his 14.3 aDOT was fourth-best among 76 WRs with at least 50 targets last year, but he was still a solid 19th in targets-per-game with 7.3 (and 19th in TPRR). From Weeks 1-8, when Odunze was healthier than not, he commanded an excellent 27.5% first-read target share and a stellar 2.21 YPRR. Odunze has clearly been better against man coverage (a very good 2.12 YPRR), so he’s a little big-play and TD-dependent, but his YPPR against zone wasn’t really bad (1.78, 36th out of 76 WRs), so with better health and a year in the system, I see Odunze as a good bet to ascend this season, emerge as a more complete receiver, and produce WR2 digits.

__{{Christian Watson|WR|GB|23395}}__ (GB, 63) — I was all-in on Watson as my breakout player heading into 2024, and he ranked top-5 in average separation score (0.187) and route win rate (22.2%) that season, along with a sick 21.4 YPR average. But it was a nightmarish and volatile year that ended in a late-season torn ACL, so he was basically off my radar last summer. But immediately upon his return last season, I was fairly stunned by his improved hands and physicality at the catch point, and he posted the best catch rate of his career (63.3%) while maintaining a high 17.5 YPR average. He was truly “commanding the ball” in this offense, which is saying something, given the Packers had a plethora of strong receiving options, and he produced against man coverage (2.55 YPRR) and zone coverage (2.87). There are two fewer options now with __Romeo Doubs__ and __Dontayvion Wicks__ off the roster, and I get the sense that HC __Matt LaFleur__ is finally ready to actually feature his best receivers, namely Watson, who is, by far, their best option at the “X” receiver spot. Watson won’t likely be a high-volume receiver on the 2026 Packers, but he was only 51st in the NFL last season in targets-per-routes-run, so his volume is set to rise on a thinned-out Packers’ receiving corps. Watson has scored 20 TDs on only 133 career receptions, which is an excellent 15% TD rate, and it’s up to 17% if we remove his injury-plagued 2024 campaign. A WR1 season may be inevitable if he can avoid injury.

__{{Alec Pierce|WR|IND|23232}}__ (Ind, 67) — With the Colts letting __Michael Pittman__ go and signing Pierce to a four-year contract extension worth up to $116 million, I’m surprised Pierce isn’t getting a little more love (a March ankle surgery to clean up a two-year issue is likely the reason). Most know about his downfield acumen, as Pierce ended the season first in aDOT (19.4), YPR (21.34), and YPT (11.94), and fourth in air yards share (43%) among 76 WRs who saw 50+ targets, and he’s averaged a ridiculous 18.7 YPR through his first four seasons. But he showed a more complete skill set in his fourth season, and the Colts clearly believe that his game will continue to expand with more volume. He has ideal size at 6’3”, 211 pounds, and his hands are excellent, which helps him in contested catch situations, so unless __Daniel Jones__ goes down again, I feel very good about Pierce’s ability to deliver a solid ROI as a 6th round pick.

__{{Ricky Pearsall|WR|SF|24982}}__ (SF, 94) — Whether you believe in the “injury-prone” label or not, the fact is, Pearsall’s been hurt a lot ( i.e. prone to injury). But he’s also only 25 years old (26 on 9/9), and fellow starter __Mike Evans__ is seven years older. Evans has had recurring hamstring strains since 2019, and such soft-tissue problems usually worsen with age. Pearsall still needs to find a way to avoid and/or play through injury himself, but if he can, he’s done very well with volume. In eight career games with six or more targets, Pearsall has put up 4/73/1, 8/141/1, 6/69/1, 4/108, 4/56, 8/117, 6/96, and 5/85. That’s 16.85 FPG, which would have ranked as the WR8 on the season last year. If you take his six healthy games with five or more targets in ‘25, Pearsall was 5th in the NFL with 2.75 YPPR. This is all worth noting because the 49ers have 143 vacated targets this year from the departed __Jauan Jennings__ and __Kendrick Bourne__. Ricky was also 4th in the league with 4.29 YPRR against man coverage in that span, along with 2.64 YPRR vs. zone (9th-best). Among 109 WRs with 200+ routes run, he was third in Win Rate and eighth in separation score, so his data when he plays healthy is excellent. The Niners have a great offense, but some of Ricky’s success is tied to SF’s low percentage of “11 personnel” with three wideouts on the field, which should continue with FB __Kyle Juszczyk__ ingrained in the offense. As for star TE __George Kittle__, he’s coming off a very serious and very late-season torn Achilles, and while his targeted return in Week 1 is realistic as of late June, I don’t think we can expect to see anything resembling peak Kittle in 2026.

__{{Michael Pittman|WR|PIT}}__ (Pit, 99) — I’ve been a __D.K. Metcalf__ hater from Day One, and I was a big Pittman guy coming out, so I’m naturally favoring the former Colt this year over the former Seahawk. Metcalf used to crush man coverage, but in 2025, his 1.46 YPPR against man was only 43rd out of 76 WRs with at least 50 targets. Meanwhile, his 2.40 YPPR against zone was 16th-best last year. The problem is, Metcalf is going to get more downfield looks this year, and that’s a problem with __Aaron Rodgers__, who was 59th (!!) at QB last year with a 6.2 aDOT, and he was 46th at QB in deep throw percentage (9.4%). So basically, with 40% of their 2025 targets gone (third most), I expect Pittman, who saw about 90% of his targets in the short/intermediate area, to be their volume receiver. I’ve interacted with Pittman several times and he’s an old soul whose father played in the league with Rodgers, so I’m very confident that Rodgers will love him.

__{{Josh Downs|WR|IND|24145}}__ (Ind, 115) — Injuries are definitely a concern for the diminutive Downs, who has dealt with thigh, hamstring, shoulder, toe, ankle, and knee issues in the NFL. But balancing the upside if he can enjoy improved health along with his downside if injuries persist, I think he’s a good pick. Downs ran only 18.5% of his routes from the outside last season, but __Michael Pittman__ and his 345 outside routes are gone (as is __A.D. Mitchell__, who was traded after playing eight games with the Colts last year). Indy signed veteran __Nick Westbrook-Ikhine__, but he’s more of a downfield specialist, and Downs is the more skilled receiver, so unless they sign a guy like __Keenan Allen__, Downs is expected to soak up some of the reps outside in 12 personnel, which is a big development for the usually slot-centric receiver. It also helps explain how we’re projecting 768.3 receiving yards at Fantasy Points, which is a healthy 18.2% higher than this total.

__{{Jalen McMillan|WR|TB|25098}}__ (TB, 160) — Of all the people on my initial list this year, I can see McMillan making the biggest leap in terms of ADP come August. But even if his stock rises 3-4 full rounds, I still think he’s a value. McMillan really flashed as a rookie with 8 TDs on only 58 targets, and while his sophomore season was ruined by a serious neck issue, he managed to catch 12 of 15 targets (80% catch rate) while averaging a healthy 14.5 YPR and leading the team with 2.41 YPPR. With Mike Evans off the roster, McMillon will likely play mostly outside, where he lined up 78% of the time last year, but he does have strong inside-outside versatility. He’s clicked well with Baker Mayfield, so I would not be shocked if McMillan winds up being their second-leading receiver — or even number one.

##### 200+ ADP guys I like

+   __{{Ryan Flournoy|WR|DAL|25124}}__ (Dal, 201) — Flashed last season and is a __George Pickens__ issue away from being an explosive breakout candidate.

+   __{{Calvin Ridley|WR|TEN|19802}}__ (Ten, 204) — Now properly cast as a #2 wideout, he should consistently get downfield opportunities as long as he’s healthy.

+   __{{Darnell Mooney|WR|NYG|21961}}__ (NYG, 209) — I’m usually in on Mooney because I think he’s good and he’s always so cheap, but last year was a disaster due to injury. But given __Malik Nabers'__ injury and the loss of __Wan’Dale Robinson__, I see a healthy Mooney, with inside-outside versatility, as a major factor in their passing game.

### __Guru’s Top 2026 Tight End Targets__

__{{Brock Bowers|TE|LV|24943}}__ (LV, 21) — The timing looks ideal for Bowers to return great value as a 2nd-round fantasy pick, since he’s coming off an injury-marred season that was also disrupted majorly due to poor QB play and a horrible offense. In theory, all three negatives have been resolved, since Bowers is expected to be 100% and ready to go for training camp. He also now has a dynamic offensive mind running the show in new HC __Klint Kubiak__, who has called Bowers a “football robot from heaven.” And finally, between QBs __Kirk Cousins__ and __Fernando Mendoza__, not to mention a prized FA pickup in C __Tyler Linderbaum__, the overall competence of the offense should rise considerably. The Raiders are high on former Viking __Jalen Nailor__, and he is a viable “sleeper” this year, but make no mistake: the passing game will go through Bowers, who will likely draw a huge contract extension at season’s end if he has a big year. With an ADP around 20, fantasy managers can select a stud RB or WR in Round 1, add Bowers in Round 2, and still likely get an excellent asset early in Round 3.

__{{Tyler Warren|TE|IND|25874}}__ (Ind, 60) — Warren, as a rookie last year, was fifth in route share (79.9%), third in targets (106), and sixth in target-per-game (6.2) and target share (19.4%) — and now veteran __Michael Pittman__ and his 19.7% target share last year is off the roster. Pittman will be replaced by __Nick Westbrook-Ikhine__, who’s never had more than 38 catches in a season, so I think it’s fair to expect Warren’s usage to increase in year two. Warren was only 21st in the team's TD percentage, and a little TD love, along with minimal time missed, should result in an elite season. If __Daniel Jones__ is able to play in 14+ games, then Warren looks like a league-winner at his 5th round ADP.

__{{Tucker Kraft|TE|GB|24118}}__ (GB, 76) — With veterans __Romeo Doubs__ and __Dontavian Wicks__ off the roster, that leaves a 28.5% target share open and up for grabs in Green Bay, which is notable because Kraft was only 14th in TE target percentage and only 18th at his position with a 69.3% route share. Even worse, he was only 23rd at TE with .22 TPRR last year. His QB __Jordan Love__ trusts him majorly, which is notable because his volume is increasing this year for sure. Among 54 TEs with at least 25 targets, Kraft was second with .62 FP/RR, and he was third at the position with a stellar 2.54 YPRR, so his potential is blatantly obvious.

__{{Sam LaPorta|TE|DET|23141}}__ (Det, 91) — LaPorta is coming off an injury-marred season, but considering his high-end ability and a limited target tree in Detroit, he could be the best TE value on the board this year. In 2025, __Jameson Williams__ averaged 7.0 targets, 79.4 receiving yards, and 15.1 FPG in eight games with LaPorta inactive. But with LaPorta active, Jamo saw only 4.8 targets, 52.7 receiving yards, and 10.9 FPG, so LaPorta may simply need to be available to come through. If healthy, he should match his 76.8% route share from ‘25, since the Lions have added only veteran slot receiver __Greg Dortch__ this offseason (and they lost veteran slot receiver __Kalif Raymond__). And in 18 career games with a route share of 75% or higher, LaPorta has averaged 15.9 FPG, which would have been good for TE2 in FPG last season. They’ve lost some players on defense, like LB __Alex Anzalone__ and CB __Amik Robertson__ (not to mention __Terrion Arnold__), plus they should lose some juice in the backfield with __David Montgomery__ gone, so we should get a slight uptick in terms of pass attempts. He may be fairly TD-dependent, but LaPorta should clearly be the third option in the passing game, and he is due for some scoring regression, since his 11.6% TD rate from 2023-2024 was down to only 7.5% last year.

__{{Travis Kelce|TE|KC|15048}}__ (KC, 110) — I’m usually out on old heads, but Kelce was on my list last year, and despite the __Patrick Mahomes__ injury that left the team with a hopeless situation at QB, Kelce was still the TE3 in total scoring and the TE9 in FPG (11.4 FPG). However, if you exclude Weeks 16, 17, and 18 without Mahomes, Kelce was his usual elite self with 12.8 FPG, which was good for TE5 in FPG. There will be a newfound affinity for the running game with OC __Eric Bieniemy__ back in the building, but Kelce is thrilled that he’s back, and there’s usually a connection between a commitment to the run and TE production. Hell, for all we know, Kelce may have retired if he had to deal with __Matt Nagy__ again, so I see no reason why Kelce can’t have yet another strong season at 37 years old, which is exactly what fellow all-time great __Tony Gonzalez__ did in his final season (83/859/8).

__{{Jake Ferguson|TE|DAL|23138}}__ (DAL, 112) — Intriguing young WR __Ryan Flournoy__ played well last year, but Ferguson still looks like the third option in the passing game in Dallas. There’s excellent continuity in Dallas with HC __Brian Schottenheimer__ entering year two and 10-year starter __Dak Prescott__ working behind an OL that is returning all five starters, including three Round 1 selections. And if George Pickens has any problems playing under the franchise tag, then the team’s reliance on Ferguson will increase.

__{{Mark Andrews|TE|BAL|19803}}__ (Bal, 121) — It’s fair to say that Andrews is slowing down, and his Average Separation Scores declined in 2025 compared to 2024. Of course, Baltimore also lost TEs __Isaiah Likely__ and __Charlie Kolar__ and will try to break in a pair of rookie TEs drafted in the fourth and fifth rounds with veteran blocking TE __Durham Smythe__ (4 receptions in 17 games last year in Chicago) in line to play a lot this year. Andrews ran 70% of his routes from the slot last season, and his Average Separation Score was still ninth-best among 69 TEs with 100 routes, while his Win Rate was seventh-best, better than __Kyle Pitts__, __Colston Loveland__, and __Trey McBride__. He’ll be 31 in September, and there is a potential out in his contract after 2026, but the club signed him to a three-year, $39.3 million contract extension this past December with over $20 million guaranteed, so they’re counting on him majorly at least this year. And since they’ll be working two rookie wideouts in a weakened receiving corps this year, __Lamar Jackson__ should be counting on his boy Andrews to be his security blanket.

__{{Brenton Strange|TE|JAX|24223}}__ (Jax, 139) — As the TE18 off the board, Strange was my “sleeper TE” pick for 2025, and if we remove his Week 5 game in which he was injured and played only 38% of the snaps (1 catch for 22 yards), he was the TE7 in total scoring and the TE11 in FPG in the 11 games he played in. He was eighth in catches (45) and fifth in receiving yards (518) with a higher YPR average than luminaries like __Harold Fannin__, __Tyler Warren__, and __Brock Bowers__. There’s a lot of hype about WRs __Brian Thomas__, __Jakobi Meyers__, and __Parker Washington__ this year and rightfully so, but the Jags just gave him a fat contract extension in June, and Trevor loves him, so I still see Strange as being sneaky-productive.

##### 200+ ADP guys I like

+   __{{Greg Dulcich|TE|MIA|23310}}__ (Mia, 210) — Athletic and still young, he could easily settle in as a top-2 target for __Malik Willis__, so the potential ROI is too good to pass up after he finished SECOND in YPRR last year among 139 qualifying TEs at 2.64.
